title: Théorie des cycles algébriques : conjectures de Hodge, Tate, Lefschetz, Weil : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
Context. The notes set up an 'Albanese equivalence' on cycles. A cycle class on X is called alg-equivalent to 0 in this strong (Albanese) sense if it is of the form Z(n). Here T is a smooth projective connected variety, Z is a correspondence (cycle) on X×T, and n is a 0-cycle on T of degree 0 whose Albanese sum S_T(n) ∈ Alb_T(k) vanishes. A^*(X) is the resulting quotient ring of cycles. The next page calls these 'classes de cycles mod équiv. d'Alb.', written A^i_alb.

(1) Top of page: end of the proof of Thm 1.4(ii), that a divisor which is Albanese-trivial is linearly trivial. Let Z be a divisor on X×T. Then t ↦ Z_t − Z_{t0} is a morphism T → Pic^0_X. By the universal property of the Albanese it factors through a homomorphism of abelian varieties u: A_T = Alb_T → Pic^0_X. For n of degree 0 one gets Z(n) = u(S_T(n)) in Pic(X). Hence S_T(n) = 0 implies Z(n) ~_lin 0. This is the classical argument that, for divisors, algebraic equivalence modulo torsion-free Albanese data coincides with linear equivalence (Matsusaka/Weil-type).

(2) Theorem 1.6. For X smooth, if z and z' in A^*(X) are both alg-equivalent to 0, then z·z' = 0 in A^*(X), i.e. the product is Albanese-trivial.

Proof sketch, as stated. Write z = Z((x)−(y)) with x, y ∈ T, and z' = Z'((x')−(y')) with x', y' ∈ T'. One may take T and T' to be curves (circled note: 'des courbes si on veut!'). Then
z·z' = W(n), where W = pr_{XT}^*Z · pr_{XT'}^*Z' on X×T×T',
and n = ((x)−(y))×((x')−(y')) = (x,x')−(x,y')−(y,x')+(y,y'), a degree-0 0-cycle on T×T'.
Since Alb(T×T') = Alb T × Alb T', one has S_{T×T'}(n) = 0. In each factor the contributions cancel, e.g. a(x)−a(x)−a(y)+a(y) = 0. So z·z' is Albanese-trivial by definition. In modern terms: F^1·F^1 ⊂ F^2, where F^1 = algebraically trivial and F^2 = 'Albanese-trivial'.

Bracketed question (with ??). If X is projective, does it suffice that one factor be alg-trivial and the other only numerically trivial?

Margin NB. 'On ignore si ce n est lin. équiv. à 0, même si T, T' sont des courbes!' This asks whether the exterior product (x−y)×(x'−y') of degree-0 cycles on a product of curves is rationally equivalent to 0.

Final remark. 'Il y a intérêt à transformer la linéarité en un énoncé sur l'opération ×': recast the linearity (Albanese) condition as a statement about exterior products.
errors: No mathematical error. In 1.6 the hypothesis 'lisse projective' was struck to leave only smoothness. The definition still uses smooth projective parameter varieties T, as the added marginal phrase says. Intersecting cycles on X then needs only smoothness, so this is consistent.

The proof is only sketched. One needs that alg-trivial classes are sums of classes Z((x)−(y)) and that intersection products commute with correspondences (W(n) = Z(·)·Z'(·)). Both are routine but unstated.

The NB question (is (x−y)×(x'−y') rationally trivial on a product of curves?) was answered negatively in general a few years later. Mumford's 1968 theorem shows the Albanese kernel T(C×C') is huge once both genera are positive (p_g>0). Bloch's work identifies such product cycles as generating it, and they are not rationally trivial in general.

ideas.what: Albanese-trivial divisors are linearly trivial via the homomorphism u: Alb_T → Pic^0_X induced by a divisorial correspondence
ideas.modern_name: Universal property of the Albanese; algebraic vs linear equivalence of divisors
ideas.where_published: FGA (Picard scheme, Exp. V-VI) in essence; SGA 6 Exp. XIII (Kleiman) for equivalence relations

ideas.what: 'Albanese equivalence' on cycles: Z(n) with n a degree-0, Albanese-sum-zero 0-cycle on a smooth projective T
ideas.modern_name: Albanese / Abel-Jacobi-type adequate equivalence; second step of the Bloch-Beilinson-type filtration
ideas.usually_credited_to: Samuel (relations d'équivalence, 1958) for general adequate relations; later Bloch, Beauville, Murre, S. Saito for the filtration viewpoint
ideas.where_published: unsure; possibly echoed in Kleiman's exposition of Grothendieck's standard conjectures (Dix exposés, 1968)

ideas.what: Product of two algebraically trivial classes is Albanese-trivial, via the exterior product (x−y)×(x'−y') having zero Albanese sum on T×T'
ideas.modern_name: F^1·F^1 ⊂ F^2 for the (conjectural) Bloch-Beilinson filtration; Albanese kernel contains exterior products of degree-0 cycles
ideas.usually_credited_to: Bloch (1970s, Albanese kernel of products of curves), S. Saito, Beauville, Murre

ideas.what: Question whether (x−y)×(x'−y') is rationally trivial on a product of curves
ideas.modern_name: Non-triviality of the Albanese kernel T(C×C'); Mumford's infinite-dimensionality theorem; Bloch's conjecture

ideas.what: Question: is (alg-trivial)·(num-trivial) Albanese-trivial on projective X?
ideas.modern_name: Multiplicativity of filtrations on Chow groups; interaction of the Griffiths group with the Albanese filtration
ideas.usually_credited_to: open-type question; related to Bloch-Beilinson / Murre conjectures

missed.claim: Grothendieck asks whether the product of an algebraically trivial class and a merely numerically trivial class (e.g. a Griffiths-type cycle) is already Albanese-trivial. This sharpens F^1·F^1 ⊂ F^2 to an 'alg × num' statement. I am not aware of this exact question being formulated in the literature.
missed.quote: Si X est projective, alors il suffit que l'un des z soit alg. équiv. à 0, et l'autre num. équiv. à 0 ??
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It concerns how Griffiths groups (num/hom-trivial but not alg-trivial cycles) multiply with algebraically trivial ones in the Bloch-Beilinson-Murre filtration. This interaction is studied (e.g. by Voisin) but the precise question seems open or unrecorded.

missed.claim: As early as c.1965-71, Grothendieck explicitly proves that products of algebraically trivial cycles land in the 'Albanese-trivial' part. He also asks whether exterior products of degree-0 cycles on products of curves are rationally trivial. This prefigures the Bloch/Mumford Albanese-kernel story and the multiplicativity of the Bloch-Beilinson filtration.
missed.quote: NB. On ignore si ce n est lin. équiv. à 0, même si T, T' sont des courbes!
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical: it shows Grothendieck isolating the Albanese kernel of C×C' and the F^1·F^1 ⊂ F^2 principle before Mumford (1968) and Bloch. This is not usually credited to him.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is elementary. Historically, though, it records Grothendieck formulating an Albanese equivalence, proving F^1·F^1 ⊂ F^2, and explicitly raising the question later settled by Mumford/Bloch on products of curves. It also poses a seemingly unrecorded 'alg × num' question. Notable but not a hidden theorem.
transcription_corrections: Theorem number: '1.6' is written over a '5' (renumbered).
In 'u : [-A_T-] A_T → Pic^0_X' the struck symbol is probably an earlier 'Alb' or 'A'; the target is \underline{Pic}^0_X.
Left margin (vertical, partly illegible) reads roughly: 'Pour voir si zz' alg. équiv. à 0, il suffit que l'un des z soit alg. équiv. à 0, l'autre ... [num.?] équiv. à 0 ...'.
NB margin: 'On ignore si ce n est lin. équiv. à 0, même si T, T' sont des courbes!' ('ceci n' → 'ce n').
